title: The Criollo Governor: Three Terms, Fifty Cows, and the Men on the Plain Who Answered to Nobody
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Asunción, the birth in the house of Sanabria
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia gives 10 September 1561; the Spanish Wikipedia infobox and the Real Academia de la Historia give 10 September 1564, while the Spanish article's body text and EcuRed give 1561. Unresolved here.
stops.campa: A son is born in Asunción to Martín Suárez de Toledo and María de Sanabria, into the lineage that founded Paraguay and then kept it. The city is a quarter-century old, adobe and cane at the far upstream end of everything Spain holds on this river. No man born on this side of the ocean has yet governed a Spanish province in his own name. This one will govern the largest of them three times, and cut it in half on his way out. The sources cannot agree whether the year is 1561 or 1564, and the atlas does not make them agree.
suggested_refs: The colonial casco historico of Asunción, seat of the Sanabria and Suárez de Toledo households
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Garay lays the city out a second time
stops.date_confidence: attested for the refoundation; the presence of the young Hernandarias is tradition only, carried by later biographers and by no muster roll
stops.campa: Juan de Garay comes down from Asunción with sixty families and founds Buenos Aires a second time, on the ground Pedro de Mendoza's people abandoned to hunger forty-four years earlier. The horses loosed on the plain in that first failure have been breeding out there in the grass ever since, ownerless. Argentine tradition puts the young Hernandarias among these settlers. No muster roll names him and his first documented office lies three years ahead across the Andes, so the atlas holds him here the way tradition holds him, at the edge of a square he will one day govern from.
suggested_refs: Juan de Garay's 1580 traza of Buenos Aires and the plaza that becomes the Plaza de Mayo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the marriage into the house of Garay
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unknown; the sources give the place only as the Río de la Plata region, so the pin falls on the canonical seat of the province
stops.campa: He marries Jerónima de Garay y Becerra Contreras Mendoza, daughter of the conquistador who laid out Buenos Aires and Santa Fe both. Garay is his father-in-law, not the uncle that later summaries keep making of him. Three daughters follow, Jerónima, Isabel and María, whose birth years no source consulted records. A criollo of twenty from Asunción is now son-in-law to the man who laid out both of the towns that hold the river, and he will hold offices in each of them.
suggested_refs: The Garay family estancia holdings at Santa Fe, later the source of the 1611 cattle

stops.name: Mendoza, corregidor of Cuyo
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: At about twenty he takes his first independent command, corregidor of Cuyo, succeeding Alonso de Miranda in the trans-Andean district then attached to the governorship of Chile. It is a long way from the river towns: vineyards and irrigation ditches under the snow line, a province administered across a cordillera from a capital on the other ocean. He holds it three years, until Juan Martínez Palomeque replaces him in 1586, and comes back east over the cordillera with the district administered and handed on whole to the man who follows him.
suggested_refs: The corregimiento of Cuyo under the gobernacion de Chile, and the early cabildo of Mendoza
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

stops.name: Concepción del Bermejo, first alcalde ordinario
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the Chaco frontier he takes part in the founding of Concepción del Bermejo, sixty kilometres west of the river it is named for, and becomes its first alcalde ordinario. The town holds forty-six years and is destroyed by indigenous attack in 1631 and 1632. Its site then goes out of memory and is recovered twice: identified in 1943 by Alfredo Martinet as the ruins at kilometre 75 of the old Route 95, confirmed by excavation in 1970 by Eldo Morresi. The first office he holds in his own name lies now under the Chaco scrub, dug up and catalogued.
suggested_refs: The excavated ruins of Concepción de Buena Esperanza at El Destierro, Chaco
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

stops.name: Corrientes, the founding and the interim command
stops.date_confidence: attested: the founding is 3 April 1588 and his interim command runs March to 7 April 1588
stops.campa: Juan de Torres de Vera y Aragón founds the city of Corrientes on the Paraná on the third of April, and Hernandarias is among those present at the founding. For a few weeks of that same month he is its first interim teniente de gobernador, governing a town whose stakes are still fresh in the ground. He is in his middle twenties. The river system is being stitched together settlement by settlement inside his own lifetime, and he stands at four of the knots.
suggested_refs: The 1588 founding act of Corrientes and its first cabildo
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

stops.name: Asunción, teniente de gobernador
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He comes back to the city he was born in, now as its teniente de gobernador. The succession list of the province puts him in charge here from 1592 to 1594, between Juan de Torres de Vera y Aragón and Fernando de Zárate; the claim that he served under Juan Ramírez de Velasco cannot stand, since Ramírez de Velasco holds the governorship only in 1595 and 1596. Thirty years after being born in this town, the criollo administers it, and the encomenderos of Paraguay watch one of their own take the chair.
suggested_refs: The cabildo of Asunción and the succession list of the Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay'

stops.name: Asunción, the province held in the interim
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In a gap in the succession he holds the joint governorship of Río de la Plata and Paraguay for the first time, on an interim commission. An interim commission lets a criollo hold a province between two peninsular appointments without anybody in Madrid deciding whether a man born in America may hold one outright. He governs on that footing until the succession resumes, and the outright title reaches him three years later, on the seventh of December 1596.
suggested_refs: Interim commissions in the Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay, 1590s
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay'

stops.name: Santa Fe la Vieja, teniente de gobernador
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He is posted to Santa Fe, which stands then on its first site at what is now Cayastá, eighty-two kilometres north of the modern city; the town will pick itself up and move south in 1660 and 1661, long after he is dead. He knows the place through his wife's father, who founded it. He does not know that he will retire here, die here, and be buried in the Franciscan church of this town, nor that the church and the grave will go under the ground with the town when it walks away.
suggested_refs: Santa Fe la Vieja on its original site at Cayastá, before the 1660 relocation
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

segments.name: The First Governor Born in America

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first criollo governor
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the seventh of December he becomes titular governor of Río de la Plata and Paraguay: not interim, not acting, the first man born in Spanish America to hold a Spanish colonial governorship in his own name. Spanish Wikipedia and EcuRed both put the claim in exactly those words, and three republics have repeated it for four centuries. He is thirty-two, or thirty-five, depending which birth year is taken. He will hold this office three separate times across twenty-two years, and no source consulted tests the claim against other provinces.
suggested_refs: The 1596 title of governor of Río de la Plata y Paraguay, first held by an American-born subject

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first term closes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Two years and seven months, and the first term ends. What follows is a confusion that later accounts keep running backwards. Diego Rodriguez Valdés y de la Banda governs after him, not before, and dies at Santa Fe in December 1600; Francés de Beaumont holds the interim from 1600 to 1602. Philip II, whom one account has confirming this first term, has been dead since September 1598. The atlas records the tangle instead of combing it out, because the combing is what produced the error in the first place.
suggested_refs: The governor succession list of the Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay, 1596-1602
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay'

stops.name: Santa Fe la Vieja, the governor dies and the seat comes open
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Valdés y de la Banda dies at Santa Fe on the twentieth of December. The province goes to Francés de Beaumont as interim for a year and a half and then, on the first of August 1602, back to Hernandarias. This is the death that returns him to the governorship, and it returns him to the second term, not the first. In the same small town where the seat falls vacant he will himself die thirty-four years later, out of office, an old man on his own land.
suggested_refs: The death of Diego Rodriguez Valdés y de la Banda at Santa Fe, December 1600
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the second term opens
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first of August he takes the province again, for seven years, the longest of his three terms and the one in which nearly everything he is remembered for gets done: the ordinances against forced Indian labour, the first schools, the kilns that put Buenos Aires into brick, the war on contraband through the port, the tower at the Riachuelo, the reconnaissance of the far bank. He is governing a few thousand Spaniards strung out across a thousand miles of river, and he governs them by riding it.
suggested_refs: The fort of Buenos Aires as the seat of the second governorship, 1602-1609

segments.name: The Second Term: the Ordinances and the Kilns

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the ordinances against the mita
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day not given; English Wikipedia dates royal approval to Philip III in 1603 and EcuRed dates it to 1608, and the difference is not resolved here
stops.campa: He legislates against the abuses of the mita and the encomienda, the two instruments by which the conquest turns Indian bodies into labour, and he does it as a man whose standing rests on the encomenderos who put him in the chair. The crown backs the reform in 1603 by one account and in 1608 by another. In 1610 he is given the title Protector de los Naturales together with two islands, and in 1611 the ordinances of Francisco de Alfaro will regulate on the ground what he has argued for on paper.
suggested_refs: The ordinances of Francisco de Alfaro, 1611, regulating Indian labour and the reductions

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the old chapel pulled down
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He orders the demolition of the shed that serves Buenos Aires for a cathedral, calling it very old and indecent, and starts replacing adobe with brick and tile. Kilns are built. The first primary schools of the city are founded. He is not relocating a cathedral, whatever the later summaries say; he is knocking down a building and firing clay to put up one that will stand. A river town of mud is being informed, by a man born in another river town of mud, that it is going to be a city.
stops.quote_source: Hernandarias's 1603 order for the demolition of the Buenos Aires chapel, as quoted in Spanish Wikipedia, 'Catedral de Buenos Aires'
suggested_refs: The first brick kilns of Buenos Aires and the primary schools of the second governorship

stops.name: Patagonia, the search for the Ciudad de los Césares
stops.date_confidence: tradition: the episode is thinly documented, the coordinate is an approximation of the Río Negro area rather than an attested location, and the sources disagree on who took him
stops.campa: He rides a thousand kilometres south of Buenos Aires after the Ciudad de los Césares, the city of silver the south is supposed to be hiding, and to learn whether the Patagonian rivers can be navigated. He finds no city. He is taken captive and gets away again: the Real Academia de la Historia says his captors are Tehuelches, English Wikipedia says Mapuche, and neither can produce a document. The atlas carries the ride the way tradition carries it, with the ground underneath it uncertain and said to be uncertain.
suggested_refs: The legend of the Ciudad de los Césares and the early Spanish reconnaissance of Patagonia
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

stops.name: The Riachuelo, the corsairs and the tower
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: English privateers take vessels lying at anchor off Buenos Aires on the eighteenth of March. Hernandarias answers in masonry: a defensive tower at the mouth of the Matanza-Riachuelo, in the bend later called the Vuelta de Rocha, and after it a larger fort. The port that his successors will spend two centuries failing to close against contraband is at this moment a beach with a river mouth beside it and a governor standing in the mud working out where to put a gun.
suggested_refs: The Riachuelo tower and fort at the Vuelta de Rocha, later La Boca

segments.name: The Far Provinces and the End of the Second Term

stops.name: The Río Santa Lucia, six months on the far bank
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the expedition runs about six months and the exact months are not given
stops.campa: For roughly six months he crosses the country on the far bank, looking for timber, coal and cane along the waters of the Río Santa Lucia. What he finds is grass. There is almost nobody on this land and it will carry cattle better than any ground he has ridden over, and he says so in writing to Philip III. The Banda Oriental at this date is an empty coast with a name on it. He is the man who works out what it is for, four years before he does anything about it.
suggested_refs: The 1607 reconnaissance of the Banda Oriental and the Río Santa Lucia basin
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

stops.name: The mouth of the Queguay, the report to the king
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The reconnaissance runs north as far as the Queguay where it comes into the Uruguay. Spanish Wikipedia keeps the sentence: on his return he crossed to its right bank, eastward of the river Queguay. His report to the king praises this country as excellent for raising cattle. The crown does nothing about it for years, so he does it himself, with his own animals, out of his own estancia, and the pastoral economy of a future republic begins as the private act of a governor whose advice was filed and ignored.
stops.quote: a su regreso, cruzó a su margen derecha, hacia el este del río Queguay
suggested_refs: The Queguay Grande at its confluence with the Río Uruguay, eastern limit of the 1607 ride
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

stops.name: Villa Rica del Espíritu Santo, the reductions of the Guairá
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In the Guairá, then the far northern province of Paraguay and now the Brazilian state of Paraná, he arranges the establishment of Jesuit and Franciscan reductions. Villa Rica del Espíritu Santo stands at this date where the town of Fênix stands now, and will be destroyed in 1632 by the bandeirantes who come south for slaves. The reduction system that Alfaro's ordinances will regulate in 1611, and that outlives the Spanish empire in memory, is being laid out on ground Paraguay is about to lose.
suggested_refs: Villa Rica del Espíritu Santo on its 1593-1632 site at Fênix, Paraná, and the Guairá reductions

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the second term closes
stops.date_confidence: attested: 8 July 1609, not the 22 July that some summaries carry
stops.campa: Seven years, and he hands the province on. The date is the eighth of July, though a stubborn error puts it on the twenty-second. He is about forty-five, or forty-eight, and has governed three times, twice by title. He will govern once more. In the interval he is a private man with an estancia at Santa Fe and a stock of cattle on it. Two years from now those animals go down the river on his own account, with no commission behind them and no soldiers along.
suggested_refs: The close of the second governorship, 8 July 1609

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Protector de los Naturales
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The crown gives him the title Protector de los Naturales and two islands in the Uruguay. The title is what the ordinances earned him; the islands are what he will use. A man is named guardian of the Indians of a province and paid in river ground, and on that ground, within the year, he will land fifty cows, and those cows will breed into the herds that the Indians and the criollos and the mestizos of that country all live off, and fight over, for the next two hundred and fifty years.
suggested_refs: The 1610 grant of the title Protector de los Naturales with the islands of Lobos and Vizcaíno

stops.name: The pampas, the ganado cimarrón and the mancebos de la tierra
stops.date_confidence: undated: the source describes the condition as already existing in Hernandarias's time without dating it, and the stop is placed at the year of the first release
stops.campa: Out on the plain the animals that got loose from the failed and half-abandoned settlements have gone feral and are breeding past counting, and there are men out there living off them: criollos and mestizos with a horse and a knife, whom the settled towns call mozos perdidos, mozos vagabundos, mancebos de la tierra. They belong to nobody. They are not yet called gauchos, and will not be for another hundred and sixty years. The vaquerías cannot work without them and the province cannot tax them.
stops.quote: existieron los gauchos... ya desde los tiempos de Hernandarias...
stops.quote_source: Unattributed period description quoted in the gaucho historiography summary at buenosaires.gob.ar
suggested_refs: The vaquerías of the pampa and the terminology of mancebos de la tierra

stops.name: Isla del Vizcaíno, fifty cows and some bulls
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He ships fifty cows and some bulls from his own estancia at Santa Fe down the river and puts them ashore on the islands of Lobos and Vizcaíno, at the mouth of the Negro where it comes into the Uruguay. Not on the mainland, as the story is usually told, and not on one island but two. He deals with the people of the country to leave the animals be. The whole operation is recorded to the head: fifty cows, some bulls, two islands, and a man two years out of office moving stock off his own estancia.
stops.quote: En 1611 Hernandarias trasladó a las islas de Lobos y del Vizcaíno 50 vacas y algunos toros desde su estancia en Santa Fe.
suggested_refs: Isla del Vizcaíno at the mouth of the Río Negro, Río Negro department, Uruguay

stops.name: Isla San Gabriel, the herd doubled
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Six years on he does it again: fifty more animals on Isla de Lobos and fifty on Isla San Gabriel off the Colonia coast. From these releases and from earlier escapes, which no source consulted can tell apart, come the herds that fill the Banda Oriental, feed the vaquerías, pay for the smuggling and make the country worth holding. Uruguay dates its ranching economy from these cows. Two centuries later Juan Manuel de Rosas will learn his trade branding their descendants on the Salado frontier.
suggested_refs: Isla San Gabriel off Colonia del Sacramento, site of the 1617 release

segments.name: The Third Term and the División

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the third title
stops.date_confidence: contested: Spanish Wikipedia gives the title on 3 May 1615; English Wikipedia gives appointment on 7 September 1614 with assumption on 29 May 1615. The year is firm, the day is not.
stops.campa: He takes the province a third time. Spanish Wikipedia says he received the title again on the third of May 1615; English Wikipedia has him appointed the previous September and taking office on the twenty-ninth of May. The atlas does not choose between them. What holds either way is that a man born in Asunción is governing Río de la Plata and Paraguay for the third time, and that in this term he will cut the province in two and write the sentence that everything after him quotes.
stops.quote: 3 de mayo de 1615 recibió nuevamente título de gobernador
suggested_refs: The third title of governor, 1615, and the contested date of assumption

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the cathedral roof fails
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The Paraguayan timber roof of the church he had rebuilt thirteen years earlier comes near collapse and the parish moves out to San Francisco. The new building goes up between January and July of 1618, the carpenter Pascual Ramírez costing the masonry at eleven hundred pesos, and Spanish Wikipedia is explicit that Hernandarias is not the man who carries out that work: his term ends on the seventeenth of May, halfway through it. The line about building at the expense of his own estate is his, but English Wikipedia is its only warrant.
stops.quote: I have built them not just with my work and perseverance, but at the expense of my estate.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Hernandarias in English Wikipedia, 'Hernando Arias de Saavedra'; which building it refers to is not established
suggested_refs: The 1618 rebuilding of the Buenos Aires cathedral under the carpenter Pascual Ramírez

stops.name: The plain between the Paraná, the Uruguay and the Negro: the mozos perdidos
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the letter's exact date, full text and archival reference were not reached in this pass
stops.campa: Governing, he writes to the crown about the men on the plain who answer to nobody, who live off the wild cattle and cannot be taxed, conscripted or found: mozos perdidos, lost youths. The historian Emilio Coni will call this the first documented reference to the people who become the gaucho. He means it as a complaint about ungovernable subjects; it is read ever after as a birth certificate. Two centuries on, Martín Miguel de Güemes forms them into the División Infernal de Gauchos de Línea, and San Martín leaves him the northern frontier to hold with them.
stops.quote_source: Hernandarias, letter of 1617, as cited in Argentine historiography after Emilio Coni; the letter's full text was not reached
suggested_refs: Emilio Coni on the 1617 letter as the first documented reference to the gaucho
sources: pedro_de_mendoza.journey.json (canonical stop 'Hernandarias and the mozos perdidos')
web search summary attributing the reading to Emilio Coni

stops.name: Madrid, the cédula that cuts the province in two
stops.date_confidence: attested for the cédula of 16 December 1617; the sources say only that it issues from the crown, and the pin falls on the court at Madrid
stops.campa: A royal cédula of the sixteenth of December authorises dividing the joint governorship in two: Buenos Aires at the river mouth, Paraguay upstream at Asunción with Santiago de Jerez, Villa Rica and Ciudad Real. He has argued for it and he gets it. The line drawn on this paper outlives the Spanish empire, and two republics will inherit it and quarrel along it. A governor who has spent thirty years riding between the halves has concluded that they are two countries and says so to a king who agrees.
suggested_refs: The royal cédula of 16 December 1617 dividing the Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Diego de Góngora takes the seat
stops.date_confidence: attested: 17 May 1618, the day Góngora took office. Some summaries wrongly close the term in 1617, confusing it with the appointment cédula.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of May Diego de Góngora formally takes office and the third and last term ends, twenty-two years after the first began. Some accounts close it in 1617, mistaking the cédula of appointment for the handover. He is about fifty-four, or fifty-seven, and has held the province five times counting the interims. He is finished with it, and he rides north to Santa Fe with nothing in his hands. What he does for the sixteen years that follow, the record barely follows at all.
suggested_refs: Diego de Góngora, first governor of Buenos Aires after the division

stops.name: Asunción, the two governorships
stops.date_confidence: attested for implementation by 1620; the exact date of effect is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The division is formalised in 1618 and implemented by 1620. Asunción, where he was born, becomes the seat of a province in its own right, no longer the upstream half of somebody else's. Santiago de Jerez, Villa Rica and Ciudad Real go upstream with it. Buenos Aires, where he governed, keeps the river mouth, the customs house and the smuggling through it. The town he was born in and the town he governed from are separated by his last act in office, and are never administered together again.
suggested_refs: The Gobernación del Paraguay after 1620, seated at Asunción

stops.name: Santa Fe la Vieja, the years the record loses
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the retirement to Santa Fe is reported, but the chronology of these sixteen years is not documented in any source consulted, and the month is a placement only
stops.campa: Out of office he goes back to Santa Fe, to the estancia the cattle came from, and for sixteen years the record holds almost nothing. No campaigns, no cedulas, no letters that anyone has put in front of this atlas. Walter Rela's edition of his correspondence with Philip III runs to 1625 and would probably fill part of the silence; it was not opened in this pass. The gap is stated here rather than furnished. He is an old man on a river, and that is the whole of what is known.
suggested_refs: Hernandarias's estancia at Santa Fe, source of the 1611 and 1617 cattle
sources: gap noted: no source consulted documents the years 1618-1634

stops.name: Santa Fe la Vieja, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Real Academia de la Historia; English Wikipedia gives only the year. The age, 70 or 72 to 73, follows directly from the unresolved birth year.
stops.campa: He dies on the twenty-first of December at Santa Fe la Vieja, seventy years old, or seventy-two, or seventy-three: the arithmetic depends on a birth year nobody has settled. He was born in a river town a quarter-century old, before Buenos Aires existed in the form that lasted. He dies with the province split in two by the cédula he argued for, the church of Buenos Aires standing in brick where he pulled the shed down, and his cattle twenty-three years loose on the far bank.
suggested_refs: The death of Hernandarias at Santa Fe la Vieja, 21 December 1634
sources: Real Academia de la Historia, Diccionario Biográfico Español

stops.name: The Convento de San Francisco, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested for burial in the Franciscan church at Santa Fe la Vieja; the day of interment is not given and is set here at the day after death
stops.campa: He is laid in the church of the Convento de San Francisco, and his wife will be laid beside him. It is the Franciscan church of a river town of a few hundred souls at the northern edge of a province he governed three times. No cathedral in Buenos Aires, no vault in Asunción, no shipment home across the ocean: the first governor born in America is buried in America, in the smallest of the towns he served. The Franciscans keep the grave for twenty-six years, until the town itself gets up and moves south without it.
suggested_refs: The church of the Convento de San Francisco at Santa Fe la Vieja

stops.name: Santa Fe, the widow's Virgin
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Jerónima, who appears in the sources both as Jerónima de Contreras and as Jerónima de Garay y Becerra Contreras Mendoza and is one woman under two renderings of one long name, outlives him by at least eight years. On the fifth of October she gives the Franciscans an image of the Virgin, and they still have it. The estancias, the cattle, the islands and the offices all pass out of the family's hands. The image stays in the church where she put it, and is there now.
suggested_refs: The Virgin image donated by Hernandarias's widow, 5 October 1642, kept by the Franciscans of Santa Fe

stops.name: Santa Fe la Vieja, the city walks away
stops.date_confidence: attested for the abandonment; the move runs across 1660 and 1661 and no single date is given
stops.campa: The inhabitants leave and Santa Fe is rebuilt eighty kilometres south, on the site it holds today. The old town is left standing where it is. The church of San Francisco falls in, the convent falls in, the silt and the grass come over the streets, and the sepulchre of Hernandarias goes underground with everything else. The province he governed keeps his name and loses the ground he is lying in, and nobody digs for either the church or the town for two hundred and eighty-nine years.
suggested_refs: The 1660-1661 relocation of Santa Fe from Cayastá to its present site
sources: histories of Santa Fe la Vieja and Cayastá, via search summary

stops.name: Maldonado, the word written down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1771 document; the exact date within the year is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: A hundred and fifty-four years after the letter about the mozos perdidos, the word gaucho appears for the first time in an official document, at Maldonado. Between the two dates lies the whole ethnogenesis: the feral herds, the vaquerías, the hide trade, the men on horses that no governor could count. Hernandarias named a nuisance. The name shifts four times and lands at last on the figure Sarmiento will fight in print, and that Borges will tell an audience in Buenos Aires no Argentine writer is obliged to supply.

stops.name: Cayastá, Zapata Gollán opens the ground
stops.date_confidence: attested for the start of the excavations in 1949; the date of the tomb's discovery within the campaign is not given
stops.campa: The archaeologist Agustín Zapata Gollán starts digging at Cayastá and finds the streets of Santa Fe la Vieja lying where they were left in 1660. He uncovers the church of San Francisco and, inside it, the sepulchre with the remains of Hernandarias. The site becomes the Parque Arqueológico Santa Fe la Vieja, a museum standing on an excavated town. Whether those bones are still in that tomb or were later moved to a reliquary, a cathedral or a case, no source consulted says, and this atlas does not guess.
suggested_refs: The Parque Arqueológico Santa Fe la Vieja at Cayastá and the Zapata Gollán excavations

stops.name: Montevideo, the bronze on the Rambla
stops.date_confidence: attested for the decree of 8 September 1976; the monument's date of erection is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Uruguay declares the bronze of Hernandarias on the Montevideo Rambla, by the sculptor Antonio Pena, a national Historic Monument. The country doing the honouring is the one his cattle stocked. In its own national account the herds that made the Banda Oriental worth holding descend from fifty animals a governor out of office put ashore on two river islands in 1611, and the bronze is decreed on that reckoning. The monument stands facing the water he shipped them down.
suggested_refs: Antonio Pena's bronze of Hernandarias on the Montevideo Rambla, Historic Monument by decree of 8 September 1976
sources: Uruguayan heritage listing, via search summary

stops.name: The Paraná crossing, a name taken back
stops.date_confidence: attested for the renaming in 2001; the exact date within the year is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The road tunnel driven under the Paraná between Santa Fe and the city of Paraná is christened the Túnel Subfluvial Hernandarias when it opens. In 2001 it is renamed for Raúl Uranga and Carlos Sylvestre Begnis, the two provincial governors who built it, and English-language reference works go on reporting that it carries his name. He held the name for a few decades, under the same river he shipped the cattle down, and then the men who dug the hole took it off him.

stops.name: Montevideo, the letters put in order
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2001 publication; no month given
stops.campa: Walter Rela compiles the letters and memorials Hernandarias sent to Philip III and the Council of the Indies between 1600 and 1625, and the Paraguayan Embassy in Montevideo publishes them. Everything this atlas could not verify about the 1617 letter, from its wording to its archival reference, is most likely inside that volume. It was not opened in this pass. The gap is named here instead of covered over, in the same city where his bronze stands looking at the river.

stops.name: Villa Hernandarias, the name on the Entre Ríos bank
stops.date_confidence: undated: the town carries his name today and no source consulted gives its founding date; the stop is placed at the present for ordering only
stops.campa: A town on the Entre Ríos side of the Paraná carries his name and holds a bust of him. The claim that its coat of arms derives from an old seal of the governor is not carried by the source cited for it and is left here as tradition. This is the river country where the Jewish agricultural colonies are planted, where Alberto Gerchunoff loses his father to a gaucho outlaw at Moisés Ville and then writes Los gauchos judíos, folding the immigrants into the figure Hernandarias first complained about to a king.
suggested_refs: Villa Hernandarias, Entre Ríos, and its bust of the governor

stops.name: Hernandarias, Alto Paraná
stops.date_confidence: undated: the city carries his name today and no founding date is given in the sources consulted; placed at the present for ordering only
stops.campa: Paraguay names a city for him as well, in Alto Paraná, some three hundred and thirty-five kilometres from the Asunción he was born in and close to the Guairá country where he set the reductions up. A monument and a small museum in Asunción itself are reported, but the only reference found for them is an unverified social-media post, and the atlas records that as exactly what it is. The province he cut in two keeps him on both sides of the cut, in towns raised long after his death.
suggested_refs: The city of Hernandarias, Alto Paraná department, Paraguay
sources: web search summary; the Asunción monument and museum detail sourced only to an unverified social-media reference

stops.name: Asunción, thirteen pages come home
stops.date_confidence: undated: the pages themselves are dated 12 December 1598, but no source consulted gives the year of the repatriation; placed at the present for ordering only
stops.campa: Thirteen handwritten pages of the Asunción cabildo records, dated the twelfth of December 1598 and carrying his hand, are stolen from Paraguay's National Archive in the 1990s and surface at auction in New York. The Manhattan District Attorney's office sends them back after a complaint from the Foreign Ministry, the Culture Secretariat and the Archive. Aimé Tschiffely rode into that same city in gaucho dress in 1928. The governor's handwriting makes the crossing four centuries after his death and is brought home to the town he was born in.
suggested_refs: The repatriated 1598 Asunción cabildo folios bearing Hernandarias's hand
sources: news reports on the manuscript repatriation, via search summary
